courses.title: Scientific Communication Skills
courses.description: This course covers the key elements of scientific communication skills that are designed to enhance the clinical research’s ability to be successful. Topics include secrets of making good oral presentations and engaging the audience, how to write and prepare abstracts, basics of grant writing and submission, and how grants are reviewed. Course includes mock grant study section.
courses.prerequisites_text: MAS program or permission of department.

courses.subject: CLRE
courses.title: Directed Studies in Clinical Research
courses.description: Faculty member will direct a student’s study in selected professional development topics in clinical research. Specific content will be tailored to the student’s particular needs and interests. Students must make arrangements with the program and individual faculty member prior to enrolling in the course.
courses.prerequisites_text: MAS program or permission of department.

courses.subject: CLRE
courses.title: Machine Learning and Predictive Analytics in Biomedical Research
courses.description: The course introduces tools and practices for predictive modeling of binary, categorical, and continuous outcomes, using the R statistical software. The methods include linear and logistic regression using LASSO, ridge regression and elastic nets, CART, boosting, bagging, and random forests. Corequisite: CLRE 254.
courses.prerequisites_text: CLRE 253, admission to the MAS in Clinical Research Program, or consent of department.

courses.subject: CLRE
courses.title: Independent Study Project
courses.description: Students conduct a high-level clinical research project that integrates what they have learned in their formal course work. The ISP will include their course work in CLRE 295A-B and be presented as a final report that includes a complete description of the project including the study manual, study results, statistical analysis, and a discussion of the findings. Students will make an oral presentation of their ISP to their three-member ISP committee comprised of faculty and industry advisers. The ISP is an independent, creative, and scholarly activity, and students will be graded on their written and oral presentations.
courses.prerequisites_text: CLRE 295A and admission to the MAS Clinical Research Program or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Introduction to Cognitive Science
courses.description: A team-taught course highlighting development of the field and the broad range of topics covered in the major. Example topics include addiction, analogy, animal cognition, human-computer interaction, language, neuroimaging, neural networks, reasoning, robots, and real-world applications.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Introduction to Data Science
courses.description: Concepts of data and its role in science will be introduced, as well as the ideas behind data-mining, text-mining, machine learning, and graph theory, and how scientists and companies are leveraging those methods to uncover new insights into human cognition.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Cognitive Consequences of Technology
courses.description: This course examines the interrelationships of cognition and technology from the perspective of cognitive science. We address questions of importance for our increasingly technological society: How does technology shape our minds? How should what we know about our minds shape technology?

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Minds and Brains
courses.description: How damaged and normal brains influence the way humans solve problems, remember or forget, pay attention to things; how they affect our emotions, and the way we use language in daily life.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Field Methods: Studying Cognition in the Wild
courses.description: This course introduces students to multiple methods to investigate cognition and behavior in natural settings. Students will learn about ethnography, videography (video data collection, coding, and analysis), surveys design and conducting interviews, and how to move from observations to modeling.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Introduction to Research Methods
courses.description: Introduction to the scientific method. Methods of knowledge acquisition, research questions, hypotheses, operational definitions, variables, control. Observation, levels of measurement, reliability, validity. Experimentation and design: between-groups, within-subjects, quasi-experimental, factorial, single-subject. Correlational and observational studies. Ethics in research.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Introduction to Statistical Analysis
courses.description: Introduction to descriptive and inferential statistics. Tables, graphs, measures of central tendency and variability. Distributions, Z-scores, correlation, regression. Probability, sampling, logic of inferential statistics, hypothesis testing, decision theory. T-test, one and two-way Anova, nonparametric tests (Chi-square).
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 14A.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Neurobiology of Cognition
courses.description: Introduction to the organization and functions of the nervous system. Topics include molecular, cellular, developmental, systems, and behavioral neurobiology. Specifically, structure and function of neurons, peripheral and central nervous systems, sensory, motor, and control systems, learning and memory mechanisms. (Students may not receive credit for both BILD12 and COGS 17. This course fulfills general-education requirements for Marshall and Roosevelt Colleges as well as Warren by petition.)

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Introduction to Python
courses.description: This class will teach fundamental Python programming skills and practices, including the “Zen of Python.” Students will focus on scientific computing and learn to write functions and tests, as well as how to debug code using the Jupyter Notebook programming environment. Students may receive credit for one of the following: BILD 62, COGS 18, CSE 8A, or CSE 6R. Recommended preparation: students with limited computing experience may take COGS 3.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: First-year Seminar
courses.description: The First-year Student Seminar Program is designed to provide new students with the opportunity to explore an intellectual topic with a faculty member in a small seminar setting. First-year Seminars can be offered in all campus departments and undergraduate colleges, and topics vary from quarter to quarter. Enrollment is limited to fifteen to twenty students, with preference given to entering first-year students.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Independent Study
courses.description: Independent literature or laboratory research by arrangement with and under direction of a Department of Cognitive Science faculty member.
courses.prerequisites_text: lower-division standing, completion of thirty units of UC San Diego undergraduate study, a minimum UC San Diego GPA of 3.0, and a completed and approved Special Studies form.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Cyborgs Now and in the Future
courses.description: Covers the theories of situated, distributed, enactive, and embodied cognition. Explains how cyborgs are a natural consequence of our current understanding of embodied minds embedded in culturally shaped niches; how mental systems can be distributed over other people and things.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 1 or COGS 10.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Sensation and Perception
courses.description: An introduction to the experimental study of cognition with a focus on sensation and perception.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 1.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Learning, Memory, and Attention
courses.description: A survey of the experimental study of learning, memory, and attention. Topics include conditioning, automaticity, divided attention, memory systems, and the nature of mental representation.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 1. Recommended: COGS 101A.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Neuroanatomy and Physiology
courses.description: This first course in the sequence focuses on principles of brain organization, from neurons to circuits to functional networks. It explores developmental plasticity, neuronal connectivity, cellular communication, complex signaling, and how these various dimensions form functional brain systems.
courses.prerequisites_text: BILD 12 or COGS 17.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Systems Neuroscience
courses.description: This course focuses on the electrical dynamics of neurons and how their patterns relate to perception, thought, and action. Neural activity patterns underlying vision, touch, audition, proprioception, and head orientation are examined in detail. Also examined are motor control, sleep/wake state production, action planning, learning, memory, attention, spatial cognition and function of the cerebellum, basal ganglia, and hippocampus.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 107A.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Data Science in Practice
courses.description: Data science is multidisciplinary, covering computer science, statistics, cognitive science and psychology, data visualization, artificial intelligence and machine learning, among others. This course teaches critical skills needed to pursue a data science career using hands-on programming and experimental challenges.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 11 or CSE 8A or COGS 18 or DSC 10 or MAE 8.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Modeling and Data Analysis
courses.description: Exposure to the basic computational methods useful throughout cognitive science. Computing basic statistics, modeling learning individuals, evolving populations, communicating agents, and corpus-based linguistics will be considered.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 14B, MATH 18 or MATH 31AH, and COGS 18 or CSE 7 or CSE 8A or CSE 11.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Beauty and the Brain
courses.description: What is beauty? The subjective experience of aesthetic appreciation dominates culture. But what determines this illusive quality? Why is it so important, how did it evolve, and how is it represented in the brain?
courses.prerequisites_text: upper-division standing.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Neurological Development and Cognitive Change
courses.description: This course provides an overview of neurological development and explores the relations between physiological change and the experience for the child from the prenatal period through adolescence.
courses.prerequisites_text: BILD 10 or BILD 12 or COGS 107A or COGS 107B or COGS 17 or HDP 110.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience
courses.description: This course will discuss the relationship between brain and cognitive development. Topics will include methods for studying the developing brain, how these methods have informed our understanding of cognitive development, the effects of environmental factors, and disorders of brain development.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 107A and COGS 107B or PSYC 106.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Neural Signal Processing
courses.description: This course will cover theoretical foundations and practical applications of signal processing to neural data. Topics include EEG/field potential methods (filtering, Fourier (spectral) analysis, coherence) and spike train analysis (reverse correlation, spike sorting, multielectrode recordings). Some applications to neural imaging (optical microscopy, fMRI) data will also be discussed.
courses.prerequisites_text: MATH 18 or MATH 31AH, COGS 14B or PSYC 60, and COGS 108 or COGS 109.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Interaction Design
courses.description: Introduces fundamental methods and principles for designing, implementing, and evaluating user interfaces. Topics: user-centered design, rapid prototyping, experimentation, direct manipulation, cognitive principles, visual design, social software, software tools. Learn by doing: work with a team on a quarter-long design project. Recommended preparation: basic familiarity with HTML. Students may not receive credit for both COGS 120 and CSE 170.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 108 or CSE 12 or DSC 30 and COGS 1 or COGS 10 or DSGN 1 or ENG 100D.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Start-up Studio
courses.description: Explores tools and processes for innovating novel business concepts to solve problems involving the interaction between humans and technology. Students will work with an interdisciplinary team to understand unmet user needs and to create a value proposition that balances technical feasibility, financial viability, and desirability.
courses.prerequisites_text: DSGN 100 or COGS 187B or COGS 187A or COGS 120 or CSE 170.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Thinking with Computers
courses.description: This course surveys the field of human-computer interaction and the ideas and technologies that have shaped its development.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 120 or COGS 121 or CSE 170.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Data-Driven UX/Product Design
courses.description: Create a UX/product design case study for your portfolio; team project with user research, data science, prototyping, and user testing. Prerequisites : VIS 41 or VIS 30 or DSGN 1 or COGS 1.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Social Cognition: A Developmental and Evolutionary Perspective
courses.description: This course presents the building blocks of social cognition from a developmental and evolutionary perspective and focuses on how and when children develop these abilities and how humans compare to other species such as great apes, birds, and dogs.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 14A-B.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Language Comprehension
courses.description: The processes and representations involved in understanding language—processing words, syntax, semantics, and discourse—are examined in light of evidence from both psychological experiments and computer simulations.
courses.prerequisites_text: upper-division standing.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Gesture and Cognition
courses.description: Spontaneous gestures and their relationship to speech, cognition, brain, and culture. The course covers, among others, gesture and language development, gesture and conceptual systems, speech-gesture coproduction and its brain bases, evolution of language, and gestural behavior in special populations.
courses.prerequisites_text: upper-division standing.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Language Development
courses.description: A comprehensive survey of theory, method and research findings on language development in children ranging from the earliest stages of speech perception and communication at birth to refinements in narrative discourse and conventional fluency through middle childhood and adolescence.
courses.prerequisites_text: upper-division standing and background in development psychology and/or linguistics is recommended.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Bilingual Minds and Brains
courses.description: This course will bring together recent discoveries about bilingualism and its influences on the brain, mind, and behavior.
courses.prerequisites_text: upper-division standing.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Upper-Division Seminar on Special Topics
courses.description: Special topics in cognitive science are discussed. (May be repeated when topics vary.)
courses.prerequisites_text: department approval.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Neurobiology of Motivation
courses.description: This course will address principles of motivation, valuation, and reward, spanning a large territory of topics, from rules of synaptic learning to classroom learning. Recommended preparation: courses in basic biology, physiology, COGS 107A or 107B or 107C, or courses in education.
courses.prerequisites_text: upper-division standing.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Space and Time in the Brain
courses.description: The course examines features of neural dynamics that map spatial and temporal relationships. Lectures will cover interval timing, mapping of item-to-observer position, mapping of observer-to-world position, and the conjunction of spatial and temporal coding in hippocampus.
courses.prerequisites_text: upper-division standing.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Neural Networks and Deep Learning
courses.description: This course will cover the basics about neural networks, as well as recent developments in deep learning including deep belief nets, convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, long-short term memory, and reinforcement learning. We will study details of the deep learning architectures with a focus on learning end-to-end models for these tasks, particularly image classification. Students may receive credit for one of the following: COGS 181, CSE 151B, or CSE 154.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 18 or CSE 11 or CSE 8B and MATH 18 or MATH 31AH and MATH 20E and MATH 180A and COGS 118A or COGS 118B or CSE 150 or CSE 151A or CSE 158 or ECE 174 or ECE 175A.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Practicum in Professional Web Design
courses.description: This course follows up on the basics of multimedia design taught in COGS 187A. Students will probe more deeply into selective topics, such as animation, navigation, graphical display of information, and narrative coherence.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 187A or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Artificial Intelligence Algorithms
courses.description: This class will cover a broad spectrum of machine learning algorithms. It builds on students’ previous exposure to machine learning. It covers new artificial intelligence algorithms ranging from topic models as used in the text data analysis to genetic algorithms. Students will not receive credit for both COGS 188 and CSE 151A.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 109 or COGS 118A or COGS 118B.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Brain Computer Interfaces
courses.description: This course will discuss signal processing, pattern recognition algorithms, and human-computer interaction issues in EEG-based brain-computer interfaces. Other types of brain-computer interfaces will also be discussed.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 108 or COGS 109 or COGS 118A or COGS 118B.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Honors Studies in Cognitive Science
courses.description: This course will allow cognitive science honors students to explore advanced issues in the field of cognitive science research. It will also provide the opportunity to develop a thesis on the topic of their choice and begin work under faculty supervision. See “ Cognitive Science Honors Program ” section for more information.
courses.prerequisites_text: COGS 190A and formal admittance to the Cognitive Science Honors Program; department stamp.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Cognitive Science Career Seminar
courses.description: This course emphasizes career readiness, with a focus on practical training in professional skills, networking, and career development. Students will be able to engage with professionals in many domains to learn how their educational breadth provides them with career advantages.
courses.prerequisites_text: junior and senior standing.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Cognitive Science Internship
courses.description: The student will undertake a program of practical research in a supervised work environment. Topics to be researched may vary, but in each case the course will provide skills for carrying out these studies. P/NP grades only. May be taken for credit up to three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: upper-division standing; 2.5 GPA; department approval.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Directed Group Study
courses.description: This independent study course is for small groups of advanced students who wish to complete a one-quarter reading or research project under the mentorship of a faculty member. Students should contact faculty whose research interests them to discuss possible projects. P/NP grades only. May be taken for credit three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: upper-division standing; 2.5 GPA; consent of instructor and department approval.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Special Project
courses.description: This independent study course is for individual, advanced students who wish to complete a one-quarter reading or research project under the mentorship of a faculty member. Students should contact faculty whose research interests them to discuss possible projects. P/NP grades only. May be taken for credit three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: upper-division standing; 2.5 GPA; consent of instructor and department approval.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Introduction to Thesis Research
courses.description: This course is taken to focus the students’ development of a thesis topic and research proposal. Students prepare an outline of thesis proposal and make an oral public presentation of the proposed topic prior to the end of the third year. S/U only.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Introduction to Research
courses.description: This sequence is an intensive research project. Students under faculty mentorship perform a thorough analysis of the problem and the literature, carry out original studies, and prepare oral and written presentations. Students should aim for a report of publishable quality. Letter grade required.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Research Methods in Cognitive Science
courses.description: Issues in design, implementation, and evaluation of research in cognitive science are discussed. Students will present and comment on their own research projects in progress. Discussions also include presentations of research to various audiences, abstracts, reviews, grant process, and scientific ethics. Letter grade required.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Programming for Behavioral Sciences
courses.description: An applied hands-on programming course that focuses on the design, implementation, and analysis of experiments. Topics include experiment design, stimulus presentation, response collection, file manipulation, data analysis, display, and presentation. Course work includes both team and individual projects. Graduate students who have not programmed at all should speak with the professor beforehand.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Collective Intelligence
courses.description: Collective intelligence is the study of how individuals coordinate, collaborate, and deliberate to produce outcomes greater than any single agent can do alone. In this course, students will explore different crowdsourcing platforms and mechanisms, read and discuss foundational papers in the field, meet virtually with contemporary authors, and write a novel research proposal that could lead to publication. Recommended preparation: COGS 230 is recommended, but not required.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Design at Large
courses.description: (Cross-listed with DSGN 219 and CSE 219.) New societal challenges, cultural values, and technological opportunities are changing design, and vice versa. The seminar explores this increased scale, real-world engagement, and disruptive impact. Invited speakers from UC San Diego and beyond share cutting-edge research on interaction, design, and learning. S/U grades only. May be taken for credit up to eighteen times. Students may receive a combined total of eighteen units for COGS 229, CSE 219, and DSGN 219.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Seminar on Special Topics
courses.description: Specific topics in cognitive science are discussed. (May be repeated when topics vary.)

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Cognitive Science Laboratory Rotation
courses.description: Laboratory rotations provide students with experience in the various experimental methods used in cognitive science.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor. S/U only.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Directed Independent Study
courses.description: Students study and research selected topics under the direction of a member of the faculty.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Thesis Research
courses.description: Students are provided directed research on their dissertation topic by faculty advisers.

courses.subject: COGS
courses.title: Teaching Apprenticeship
courses.description: This practicum for graduate students provides experience in teaching undergraduate cognitive science courses. S/U only.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Introduction to Communication
courses.description: This course is an introduction to the history, theory, and practice of communication. Topics covered include language literacy, representation, semiotics, mediated technologies, institutional formations, and social interaction. Course work may involve media production (for example, writing, video and media production, or performance). No credit for COMM 10 if taken after COMM 10R.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Analysis of Audio/Visual Media: Form, Style, and Meaning
courses.description: This course builds the critical skills to understand, analyze, interpret audio/visual media by introducing students to the basic vocabulary and grammar of audio and moving image texts—how they create meaning through compositional form and narrative style—and key critical methodologies for interpreting media culture. Concepts covered will lay the groundwork for continued study in scholarly communication areas and hands-on sound, film/video, and/or social media production. No credit for COMM 20 if taken after COMM 20R.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Digital Media Literacy: Analyzing Forms, Practices, and Infrastructures of Mediated Public Life
courses.description: The role of digital communication in a democratic system, and the ways mass media both facilitate and inhibit the development of a viable public sphere. By exploring today’s digital communication dynamics, students will have the opportunity to become more mindful, active consumers of media and to feel empowered to be engaged participants in public life.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Presenting and Public Speaking
courses.description: This course covers the basics of communication in public and professional settings. Students will cultivate their own speaking style while developing skills in delivery, performance, and persuasion. They will learn how to create a slide deck as well as prepare for speeches, interviews, and Q and As.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Public Presentation and Persuasion—Speech and Debate
courses.description: Throughout history, important advances in a democratic society have emerged most often from civil, rigorous discussion, debate, and persuasion. Students develop research, critical thinking, presentation, public speaking, and argumentation skills through in-class practice speeches and debates, along with participation in intercollegiate speech and debate tournaments. May be taken for credit up to six times.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: First-year Student Seminar
courses.description: The First-year Student Seminar Program is designed to provide new students with the opportunity to explore an intellectual topic with a faculty member in a small seminar setting. First-year student seminars are offered in all campus departments and undergraduate colleges, and topics vary from quarter to quarter. Enrollment is limited to fifteen to twenty students, with preference given to entering first-year students.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Communication, Institutions, and Power
courses.description: This course is a critical introduction to structures of communication formed at the intersection of the state, the economy, and civil society. It includes a historical survey of communication and media industries; legal and policy-based arenas; and civic, political, and social organizations. Students will learn to assess the movement of power through these institutions and its effect in shaping society, culture, and politics. No credit for COMM 100C if taken after COMM 100CR.
courses.prerequisites_text: junior or senior standing.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Introduction to Audiovisual Media Practices
courses.description: This upper-division course is required as the gateway to all future communication media production courses. Students will learn about contemporary media practices such as film, video, digital/online, and social media production, and how these practices are formed by technical and social constraints. In the studio portion of this course, students will work hands-on with video and new media equipment to apply what they have learned.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: MPL: Nonlinear/Digital Editing
courses.description: This hands-on post-production course introduces students to the art and practice of editing. Approaches to montage will be analyzed, discussed, and critically applied. This course is project-intensive, and will prepare students to edit using digital non-linear editing systems. May be taken for credit three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 101 or VIS 70N.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: MPL: Documentary Sketchbook
courses.description: Digital video is the medium used in this class both as a production technology and as a device to explore the theory and practice of documentary production. Technical demonstrations, lectures, production exercises, and readings will emphasize the interrelation between production values and ethics, problems of representation, and documentary history. May be taken for credit three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and COMM 101.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: MPL: Sound Production and Manipulation
courses.description: This hands-on course serves as an introduction to sound production, design, and editing. Students create projects by recording original sounds and editing on a digital audio workstation. We consider the potential of sound in film, radio, TV, and on the web by reviewing work and reading sound theory. May be taken for credit three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 101 or VIS 70N.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: MPL: Topics in Production
courses.description: Specialized study in production with topics to be determined by the instructor for any given quarter. Students will use audio/film studios, editing rooms, and cameras to produce media work in a variety of forms for various presentation platforms that can include documentary shorts, radio plays, or digital images. May be taken for credit three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 101 or COGN 22 or VIS 70N prerequisites can be taken concurrently by permission.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: MMPP: Audio Story and Podcasting Practicum
courses.description: Production-oriented course involving diverse audio media forms. Critically analyze journalistic podcasts, features, documentaries, diaries, place-casts, and news shorts to evaluate what makes for compelling and effective audio as a contemporary storytelling form. Students will gain technical and production skills to facilitate their own creativity in the audio sphere. May be taken for credit three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and COMM 101.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: MMPP: Practicum in New Media and Community Life
courses.description: A combined lecture/lab in a specially designed after-school setting in southeastern San Diego working with children and adults. Students design new media and produce special projects, and explore issues related to human development, social justice, and community life. May be taken for credit three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: none

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: CM: Documentary History and Theory
courses.description: History of nonfiction film and video. Through film and written texts, we survey the nonfiction film genre, considering technological innovations, ethical issues, and formal movements related to these representations of the “real.”
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: CM: History of Electronic Media
courses.description: This course considers the social, cultural, economic, and technological contexts that have shaped electronic media, from the emergence of radio and television to their convergence through the internet, and how these pervasive forms of audiovisual culture have impacted American society.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Introduction to Media Industries
courses.description: Introduction to topics that arise across various media industries, including media economics, ownership and consolidation in media, media regulation and deregulation, media technologies, creative labor, intellectual property, financialization, globalization, and ethics in media. Engage directly with current events, read recent coverage in the trade press, and learn to analyze contemporary media companies and systems.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10, COMM 20, COMM 30, COMM 30GS, or COMM 40.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Advertising and Society
courses.description: Advertising as a commercial and social force. The development of advertising, branding, and consumer culture in the United States; the history and political economy of advertising in mass and digital media; semiotics and representation in advertisements; influencers, authenticity, and the monetization of self and community; subversion and rebellion within systems of advertisement and promotion.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10, COMM 20, COMM 30, COMM 30GS, or COMM 40.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Journalism and the News Industry
courses.description: Survey the development of journalism as a profession and news media as an industry and social institution. How to understand the production of news, the forces that shape social representations in the news, access to the public sphere, and approaches to the analysis of news media content. Debates about ethical issues in journalism, “objectivity” and the politics of news, and the sustainability of journalism as an institution. No credit for COMM 106N if taken after COMM 106NR.
courses.prerequisites_text: junior or senior standing.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Visual Culture
courses.description: How visual images contribute to our understanding of the world and ourselves. Theoretical approaches from media studies, art history, gender studies, and social theory will be used to analyze cultures of science, art, mass media, and everyday life.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: CCP: Communication and Cultural Production: Introduction
courses.description: This course examines the products of culture industries (e.g., music, television, fashion, food, landscape, architectural design) to analyze, specifically, how culture is consumed and by whom. How are spectators hailed and audiences fostered and shaped? And what is the role of audiences in fostering and shaping cultural forms and products?
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: CCP: Global Borders: Communication and Conflict
courses.description: Across the globe, geopolitical borders are charged sites of cross-cultural communication and conflict. While borders are commonly conceived as fixed physical demarcations, in this course we will examine borders as sites of exchange, as contested boundaries where diverse actors and practices converge and diverge, and as complex historical and socio-spatial formations that call into question presumed divisions between inside/outside, us/them, human/nonhuman, and technological/ecological.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: CCP: Performance and Cultural Studies
courses.description: Explores performance as a range of aesthetic conventions (theatre, film, performance art) and as a mode of experiencing and conveying cultural identity. Texts include critical writing from anthropology, psychology, linguistics, media studies, as well as film/video, play scripts, live performance.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Intermediate Topics in Communication
courses.description: Specialized study of communication topics, to be determined by the instructor, for any given quarter. May be taken for credit three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: CSI: Media Technologies and Social Movements
courses.description: Course explores the roles of media technologies in activist campaigns, social movements. Blending theory, historical case studies, and project-based group work, students will investigate possibilities and limitations of attempts to enroll new and old media technologies in collective efforts to make social change.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: CSI: Science Communication
courses.description: This course examines science communication as a unique form of storytelling, identifying who does science communication, how, why, and with what impacts. Through an exploration of the social construction of scientific knowledge, the course highlights science communication’s role in democracy, power, justice, public reason, technological trajectories, university-community relations, and health activism.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: AMP: Media Stereotypes
courses.description: An examination of how the media present society’s members and activities in stereotypical formats. Reasons for and consequences of this presentation are examined. Student responsibilities will be (a) participation in measurement and analysis of stereotype presentations. (b) investigating techniques for assessing both cognitive and behavioral effects of such scripted presentations on the users of media. Students will not receive credit for COMT 105 and COMM 120M.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and two of COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Critical Design Practice/Advanced Studio
courses.description: This hands-on course introduces design as social and political transformation. In it, students will learn to analyze how designed objects and environments entail political assumptions and choices, working in groups to design an intervention into some aspect of collective life that concerns them. It will include a mixture of lectures and studio-based activities.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 or COGS 1 or DSGN 1 or ESYS 10 or POLI 10 or POLI 10D or USP 1.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Media Audiences
courses.description: Examines the complex relationship between mass media and the consumers and viewers they target. This course covers theories about audiences, reading practices of audiences, the economics of audiences, and the role of audiences in the digital era.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and one from COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Black Women Filmmakers
courses.description: Students examine film and video media produced by black women filmmakers worldwide. This course will use readings from the writings of the filmmakers themselves as well as from film studies, women’s studies, literature, sociology, and history.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and one from COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Black Women, Feminism, and Media
courses.description: This course examines the challenges that arise in using feminist theory to understand black women’s experience in Africa and the United States. It also looks at the mass media and popular culture as arenas of black feminist struggle.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and one from COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: History, Memory, and Popular Culture
courses.description: What role does popular culture play in shaping and creating our shared memory of the past? The course examines diverse sources such as school textbooks, monuments, holidays and commemorations, museums, films, music, and tourist attractions.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and two from COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Advanced Topics in Cultural Production
courses.description: Specialized advanced study in cultural production with topics to be determined by the instructor for any given quarter. May be taken for credit three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and one from COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Media and Conflict Environment: Textual and Visual Representations
courses.description: Environments of conflict, including war, generate enormous amounts of passion as well as controversy. This course examines how various forms of media represent violent conflicts, and the controversies that follow from these media representations. The aim of the course is to explore how the culture, political economy, and primary actors of media environments confront the challenge of covering various types of conflicts and the types of stories and images that emerge in the process.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and one from COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Tourism and Imperialism
courses.description: This course studies tourism as a form of imperialism. It explores the industry’s role in reproducing race, gender, labor, and ecological and geographical inequalities by looking at real case scenarios from around the world. Traveling for pleasure is a privilege. For some to be able to travel, others need to stay still, working to accommodate tourists’ desires and consumption fantasies. The course offers critical tools to help us think about the future of tourism in the face of contemporary crises.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and one from COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Behind the Internet: Invisible Geographies of Power and Inequality
courses.description: This course aims to unveil the vast and largely hidden infrastructures silently shaping how digital communication take place in contemporary societies as well as the visible and invisible geographic of power and inequality these infrastructures are helping to create.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and one from COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Culture, Domination, and Resistance
courses.description: Explores theories and narratives of cultural power, contemporary practices of resistance. Texts from a wide range of disciplines consider how domination is enacted, enforced, and what modes of resistance are employed to contend with uses and abuses of political power.
courses.prerequisites_text: COMM 10 and one from COMM 100A, 100B, 100C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Junior Seminar in Communication
courses.description: The junior seminar enables a detailed examination of a specific topic from the field of communication selected by the instructor, exploring in greater depth theories and methods introduced in the core communication curriculum. Seminars are limited to thirty students with a heavy focus on class participation. Students complete a research project with a significant final product (typically a research paper). No credit for COMM 190 if taken after COMM 190R.
courses.prerequisites_text: junior or senior standing and COMM 10 and at least one from COMM 100A-B-C.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Research Seminar in Washington, D.C.
courses.description: (Same as POLI 194, USP 194, HITO 193, SOCI 194, and COGS 194) Course attached to six-unit internship taken by students participating in the UCDC program. Involves weekly seminar meetings with faculty and teaching assistants and a substantial research paper.
courses.prerequisites_text: participation in UCDC program.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Honors Seminar in Communication II: Research
courses.description: Preparation of an honors thesis, which can be either a research paper or a media production project. Open to students who have been admitted to the honors program. Grades will be awarded upon completion of the two-quarter sequence.
courses.prerequisites_text: minimum grade of B+ in COMM 196A.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Independent Study in Communication
courses.description: Independent study and research under the direction of a member of the faculty. May be taken three times for credit.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor. (P/NP grades only.)

courses.subject: COGR
courses.title: Introduction to Study of Communication: Communication and Culture
courses.description: This course focuses on questions of interpretation and meaning. This course will examine how people use texts to interpret the world and coordinate their activities in social groups. Students will study both theories of interpretation in the conventional sense and theories about the act of interpreting. Restricted to major code CM75.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: COGR
courses.title: Introduction to the Study of Communication: Communication and the Individual
courses.description: This course will draw on theorists who examine human nature as constituted by social, material, and historical circumstances. This course considers the media in relation to the ontogenetic and historical development of the human being and an examination of the individual as socially constituted in a language-using medium. The role of new communication technologies as part of research methodologies is explored in lecture-seminar. Restricted to major code CM75.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: COGR
courses.title: Comparative Analysis
courses.description: The logic of comparative analysis and its role in communication research. Scientific inference in qualitative research. Selection of cases. Problems of translation across cultures.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: COGR
courses.title: Colloquium in Science Studies
courses.description: A forum for the presentation and discussion of research in progress in science studies by graduate students, faculty, and visitors. Students must attend the colloquium series for their entire first and second years. They receive course credit in one quarter each year.
courses.prerequisites_text: enrollment in the Science Studies Program.

courses.subject: COGR
courses.title: Introduction to Science Studies Part II
courses.description: Continuing the introduction developed in Part 1, this course examines recent key topics and problem situations in science studies. Emphasis is on recent theoretical perspectives and empirical studies in communication, history, philosophy, and sociology of science and technology, and the interplay between them.
courses.prerequisites_text: completion of COGR 225A, HIGR 238, Phil 209A, or SOCG 255A or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: COGR
courses.title: Performance Theory
courses.description: Course is designed to introduce graduate students to the disciplinary, intellectual, and artistic genealogies of performance studies that bring together critical work from the fields of anthropology, art history, communication, critical gender studies, ethnic studies, film studies, literature, and theatre studies.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: COGR
courses.title: Topics in Communication
courses.description: Specialized study in communication, with topics to be determined by the instructor for any given quarter.

courses.subject: COGR
courses.title: Directed Group Study
courses.description: The study and analysis of specific topics to be developed by a small group of graduate students under the guidance of an interested faculty member.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing or consent of instructor.

courses.subject: COGR
courses.title: Graduate Research
courses.description: Advanced independent study in communication under the guidance of Department of Communication faculty.

courses.subject: COGR
courses.title: Practice Teaching in Communication
courses.description: A doctoral student in communication is required to assist in teaching undergraduate Department of Communication courses for a total of six quarters. One meeting per week with the instructor, one meeting per week with the assigned sections, and attendance at the lecture of the undergraduate course in which he or she is participating are part of this requirement.

courses.subject: CSS
courses.title: Data and Model Programming for Computational Social Science
courses.description: This course explores the use of computational methods across the social sciences. Topics include thinking like a computational social scientist; research design for big data; legal and ethical dimensions of computational social science (CSS). Students will implement demonstrations of these methods in Python.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSS 1 and choose one of the following courses: COGS 14B, MATH 11, MGT 3, POLI 30, POLI 30D, PSYC 60.

courses.subject: CSS
courses.title: Advanced Statistical Applications
courses.description: Use of advanced quantitative techniques in social science. Students will use social science data to complete small exercises and a major project.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing, CSS 204, POLI 204B, POLI 270, or PSYC 201A.

courses.subject: CSS
courses.title: Computational Social Science Research Seminar
courses.description: A weekly seminar series focused on selected topics in computational social science.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing.

courses.subject: CSS
courses.title: Research in Computational Social Science
courses.description: Independent research under the supervision of individual faculty members.
courses.prerequisites_text: graduate standing.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Programming and Computational Problem-Solving I
courses.description: Introductory course for students interested in computer science and programming. Basics of programming including variables, conditionals, loops, functions/methods. Structured data storage such as arrays/lists and dictionaries, including data mutation. Hands-on experience with designing, writing, hand-tracing, compiling or interpreting, executing, testing, and debugging programs. Students solve relevant computational problems using a high-level programming language. CSE 8A is part of a two-course sequence (CSE 8A-B) that is equivalent to CSE 11. Students should take CSE 8B to complete the CSE 8A/CSE 8B track. Students who have taken CSE 8B or CSE 11 may not take or receive credit for CSE 8A. Students may receive credit for one of the following: COGS 18, CSE 8A, or CSE 6R. Recommended preparation: No prior programming experience is assumed, but comfort using computers is helpful. Students should consult the “CSE Course Placement Advice” web page for assistance in choosing which CSE course to take first.
courses.prerequisites_text: restricted to undergraduates. Graduate students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Programming and Computational Problem-Solving: Accelerated Pace
courses.description: Accelerated introductory programming including an object-oriented approach. Covers basic programming topics from CSE 8A including variables, conditionals, loops, functions/methods, structured data storage, and mutation. Also covers topics from CSE 8B including the Java programming language, class design, interfaces, basic class hierarchies, recursion, event-based programming, and file I/O. Basics of command-line navigation for file management and running programs. Zero units of credit offered for CSE 11 if CSE 8B taken previously or concurrently. Recommended preparation: Significant prior programming experience (for example, high school AP CSA). Students should consult the “CSE Course Placement Advice” web page for assistance in choosing a first CSE course.
courses.prerequisites_text: restricted to undergraduates. Graduate students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Basic Data Structures and Object-Oriented Design
courses.description: Use and implementation of basic data structures including linked lists, stacks, and queues. Use of advanced structures such as binary trees and hash tables. Object-oriented design including interfaces, polymorphism, encapsulation, abstract data types, pre-/post-conditions. Recursion. Uses Java and Java Collections.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 8B or CSE 11; restricted to undergraduates. Graduate students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Discrete Mathematics
courses.description: This course will introduce the ways logic is used in computer science: for reasoning, as a language for specifications, and as operations in computation. Concepts include sets, relations, functions, equivalence relations, partial orders, number systems, and proof methods (especially induction and recursion). Propositional and predicate logic will be introduced and applied to various computer science domains such as circuit design, databases, cryptography, and program correctness. Students who have completed MATH 109 may not receive credit for CSE 20. Credit not offered for both MATH 15A and CSE 20. Equivalent to MATH 15A.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 11 or CSE 6R or CSE 8A or CSE 8B or ECE 15. Prerequisite courses must have been completed with a grade of C– or better; restricted to undergraduates. Graduate students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Mathematics for Algorithms and Systems
courses.description: This course will cover mathematical concepts used to model and analyze algorithms and computer systems. Topics include counting techniques (inclusion-exclusion; recursive counting; permutations and combinations), data representations, analysis of algorithms (order notation; time complexities; loop invariants), recurrence relations, graphs and trees (data structure representations; basic graph algorithms; special classes of graphs), and basic probability and its applications.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 20 or MATH 15A or MATH 31CH; students who have completed MATH 154 or MATH 184 or MATH 188 previously or concurrently may not receive credit for CSE 21; restricted to undergraduates. Graduate students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Systems Programming and Software Tools
courses.description: A programmer’s view of how computer systems execute programs, store information, and communicate. Emphasis on understanding the details of how a single computer program executes on a computer. Hands-on systems programming using the C programming language and software tools (e.g., gdb, valgrind, make) in the UNIX environment. Builds foundation for courses on computer organization, operating systems, networks, and compilers.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 11 or CSE 8B or ECE 15; two units of credit offered for CSE 29 if CSE 15L taken previously.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Computer Organization
courses.description: Introduction to organization of modern digital computers. Students learn how to write programs in assembly, design basic processors capable of executing the assembly programs, and how to build the basic components of processors using digital logic. Topics include assembly programming, combinational and sequential logic, processor performance, processor design, and the memory hierarchy.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 15L or CSE 29 or ECE 15; restricted to undergraduates. Graduate students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: First-year Student Seminar
courses.description: The First-year Student Seminar Program is designed to provide new students with the opportunity to explore an intellectual topic with a faculty member in a small seminar setting. First-year student seminars are offered in all campus departments and undergraduate colleges, and topics vary from quarter to quarter. Enrollment is limited to fifteen to twenty students, with preference given to entering first-year students.
courses.prerequisites_text: none.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Computer Science and Engineering Seminar
courses.description: A seminar format discussion led by CSE faculty on topics in central areas of computer science, concentrating on the relation among them, recent developments, and future directions. This seminar introduces incoming students to resources and opportunities in the CSE department. May be taken for credit up to three times. Restricted to students in the CSE-PACE program.
courses.prerequisites_text: none.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Tutor Apprenticeship
courses.description: Students assigned to tutor for a CSE course for the first time receive individual and group mentoring and training on how to be effective tutors to help them develop the skills and tools needed to be effective in their tutor role. Students must have a concurrent tutor appointment in a CSE course. See CSE website for application information.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Independent Study in Computer Science and Engineering
courses.description: Independent reading or research by special arrangement with a faculty member.
courses.prerequisites_text: lower-division standing. Completion of thirty units at UC San Diego with a UC San Diego GPA of 3.0. Special Studies form required. Department stamp required. Consent of instructor and approval of the department.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Advanced Data Structures
courses.description: High-performance data structures and supporting algorithms. Use and implementation of data structures like (un)balanced trees, graphs, priority queues, and hash tables. Also, memory management, pointers, recursion. Theoretical and practical performance analysis, both average case and amortized. Uses C++ and STL. Recommended preparation: background in C or C++ programming.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 21 or MATH 154 or MATH 158 or MATH 184 or MATH 188 and CSE 12 and CSE 15L or CSE 29 or ECE 15; restricted to undergraduates. Graduate students will be allowed as space permits. Students may not receive credit for both CSE 100R and CSE 100.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Advanced Data Structures
courses.description: High-performance data structures and supporting algorithms. Use and implementation of data structures like (un)balanced trees, graphs, priority queues, and hash tables. Also memory management, pointers, recursion. Theoretical and practical performance analysis, both average case and amortized. Uses C++ and STL.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 21 or MATH 154 or MATH 158 or MATH 184 or MATH 188 and CSE 12 and CSE 15L or CSE 29 or ECE 15. This course is a distance education course. Students may not receive credit for both CSE 100R and CSE 100.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
courses.description: Design and analysis of efficient algorithms with emphasis of nonnumerical algorithms such as sorting, searching, pattern matching, and graph and network algorithms. Measuring complexity of algorithms, time and storage. NP-complete problems.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 21 or MATH 154 or MATH 158 or MATH 184 or MATH 188 and CSE 12 or DSC 30; restricted to undergraduates. Graduate students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Theory of Computability
courses.description: An introduction to the mathematical theory of computability. Formal languages. Finite automata and regular expressions. Push-down automata and context-free languages. Computable or recursive functions: Turing machines, the halting problem. Undecidability.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 12 and CSE 20 or MATH 109 or MATH 15A or MATH 31CH and CSE 21 or MATH 100A or MATH 103A or MATH 154 or MATH 158 or MATH 184 or MATH 188; restricted to CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, EC26, and MA30 majors. Other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Modern Cryptography
courses.description: Topics include private and public-key cryptography, block ciphers, data encryption, authentication, key distribution and certification, pseudorandom number generators, design and analysis of protocols, zero-knowledge proofs, and advanced protocols. Emphasizes rigorous mathematical approach including formal definitions of security goals and proofs of protocol security.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 21 or MATH 154 or MATH 158 or MATH 184 or MATH 188 and CSE 101 and CSE 105; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS28, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Software Engineering
courses.description: Introduction to software development and engineering methods, including specification, design, implementation, testing, and process. An emphasis on team development, agile methods, and use of tools such as IDE’s, version control, and test harnesses.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 100 or CSE 100R; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Operating Systems Principles
courses.description: Introduces operating systems concepts, including processes, synchronization, scheduling, memory management, virtual memory, file systems, and protection. May be coscheduled with CSE 220.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 15L or CSE 29 and CSE 30 and CSE 100 or CSE 100R and CSE 101; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Wireless Networks
courses.description: This course covers the design, operation, and use of wireless technologies, with emphasis on how physical resource constraints and application constraints meet to affect link, network, system, and application design, with hands-on experience in multiple technologies. May be coscheduled with CSE 222C. Recommended preparation: Basics of software engineering, modular design, data structures, physical (in-memory) representation of data structures, code compilation, build systems, version control, debuggers, C code, and pointer manipulation in C.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 30 or ECE 30 and CSE 101 or ECE 141A and CSE 110 or ECE 141B.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Computer Security
courses.description: Topics include basic cryptography, security/threat analysis, access control, auditing, security models, distributed systems security, and theory behind common attack and defense techniques. The class will go over formal models as well as the bits and bytes of security exploits.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 21 or MATH 154 or MATH 158 or MATH 184 or MATH 188 and CSE 120 or CSE 123 or CSE 124 or ECE 158A or ECE 158B; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS28, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Programming Languages: Principles and Paradigms
courses.description: (Formerly CSE 173.) Introduction to programming languages and paradigms, the components that comprise them, and the principles of language design, all through the analysis and comparison of a variety of languages (e.g., Pascal, Ada, C++, PROLOG, ML.) Will involve programming in most languages studied.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 12 and CSE 100 or CSE 100R and CSE 105; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Database System Principles
courses.description: Basic concepts of databases, including data modeling, relational databases, query languages, optimization, dependencies, schema design, and concurrency control. Exposure to one or several commercial database systems. Advanced topics such as deductive and object-oriented databases, time allowing.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 100 or CSE 100R; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, EC26, CS27, CS28, and CS29 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Web Client Languages
courses.description: Design and implementation of interactive World Wide Web clients using helper applications and plug-ins. The main language covered will be Java.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 100 or CSE 100R; restricted to CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Components and Design Techniques for Digital Systems
courses.description: Design of Boolean logic and finite state machines; two-level, multilevel combinational logic design, combinational modules and modular networks, Mealy and Moore machines, analysis and synthesis of canonical forms, sequential modules.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 30 or ECE 30; restricted to CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Digital Systems Laboratory
courses.description: Implementation with computer-aided design tools for combinational logic minimization and state machine synthesis. Hardware construction of a small digital system.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 30; restricted to CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Computer Architecture: A Software Perspective
courses.description: This course covers the operation, structure, and programming interfaces of modern CPUs with an emphasis on exploiting processor features to improve software performance and efficiency. The topics covered in this course include performance, energy, x86 assembly, compiler optimizations, pipelining, instruction-level parallelism, caches, memory-level parallelism, multi-threading, multi-core processors, and SIMD. Two units of credit offered for CSE 142 if CSE 141 taken previously or concurrently.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 30 or ECE 30 and CSE 100 or CSE 100R. Restricted to students within CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Embedded Systems
courses.description: This course introduces the breadth of embedded systems, including hardware, software and modeling techniques. Embedded hardware topics include various types of processors and accelerators, memory, system and communication interfaces, sensors, and actuators. Embedded software includes timing, real-time and distributed scheduling, operating systems. The class will have design projects using off the shelf hardware and software components. Recommended preparation: Basic understanding of operating systems and computer architecture is strongly recommended.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 30.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Advanced Processor Architecture Design Project
courses.description: Students will use hardware description language tools to add advanced architectural features to a basic processor design. These features may include pipelining, superscalar execution, branch prediction, and advanced cache features. Designs will be implemented in programmable logic devices.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 141 or CSE 142; graduate students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence: Probabilistic Reasoning and Decision-Making
courses.description: Introduction to probabilistic models at the heart of modern artificial intelligence. Specific topics to be covered include probabilistic methods for reasoning and decision-making under uncertainty; inference and learning in Bayesian networks; prediction and planning in Markov decision processes; applications to intelligent systems, speech and natural language processing, information retrieval, and robotics.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 12 or DSC 40B and CSE 15L or CSE 29 or DSC 80 and COGS 118D or CSE 103 or ECE 109 or ECON 120A or MAE 108 or MATH 180A or MATH 180B or MATH 181A or MATH 183 or MATH 186 and MATH 20A and MATH 18 or MATH 31AH; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, EC26, and DS25 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Machine Learning: Learning Algorithms
courses.description: Broad introduction to machine learning. The topics include some topics in supervised learning, such as k-nearest neighbor classifiers, decision trees, boosting, and perceptrons; and topics in unsupervised learning, such as k-means and hierarchical clustering. In addition to the actual algorithms, the course focuses on the principles behind the algorithms. Students may not receive credit for both CSE 151A and COGS 188. May be coscheduled with CSE 251A.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 12 or DSC 40B and CSE 15L or CSE 29 or DSC 80 and COGS 118D or CSE 103 or ECE 109 or ECON 120A or MAE 108 or MATH 180A or MATH 180B or MATH 181A or MATH 183 or MATH 186 and MATH 18 or MATH 31AH and MATH 20C or MATH 31BH; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, EC26, and DS25 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Deep Learning
courses.description: This course covers the fundamentals of deep neural networks at the undergraduate level. We introduce linear regression, multi-layer perceptrons, backpropagation, and automatic differentiation. We will also discuss convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and transformers. The course will be a combination of lectures, presentations, and machine learning competitions. Renumbered from CSE 154. Students may receive credit for one of the following: CSE 151B, CSE 154, or COGS 181. May be coscheduled with CSE 251B. Recommended preparation: knowledge of Python.
courses.prerequisites_text: MATH 20C or MATH 31BH and BENG 134 or COGS 118D or CSE 103 or ECE 109 or ECON 120A or MAE 108 or MATH 180A or MATH 180B or MATH 181A or MATH 183 or MATH 186 or SE 125 and COGS 118A or COGS 118B or COGS 188 or CSE 151A or DSC 140B or ECE 175A; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS28, CS29, EC26, and DS25 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Computer Vision I
courses.description: This course provides a broad introduction to the foundations, algorithms, and applications of computer vision. It introduces classical models and contemporary methods, from image formation models to deep learning, to address problems of 3-D reconstruction and object recognition from images and video. Topics include filtering, feature detection, stereo vision, structure from motion, motion estimation, and recognition. Programming assignments will be in Python. Students may not receive credit for both CSE 152A and CSE 152.
courses.prerequisites_text: MATH 18 or MATH 31AH and CSE 12 or DSC 30 and CSE 15L or CSE 29 or DSC 80; Python programming experience recommended; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Statistical Natural Language Processing
courses.description: Natural language processing (NLP) is a field of AI which aims to equip computers with the ability to intelligently process natural (human) language. This course will explore statistical techniques for the automatic analysis of natural language data. Specific topics covered include probabilistic language models, which define probability distributions over text passages; text classification; sequence models; parsing sentences into syntactic representations; and machine translation.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 12 or DSC 40B and CSE 15L or CSE 29 or DSC 80 and BENG 134 or COGS 118D or CSE 103 or ECE 109 or ECON 120A or MAE 108 or MATH 180A or MATH 180B or MATH 181A or MATH 183 or MATH 186; restricted to students within the CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Introduction to Parallel Computing
courses.description: Introduction to high performance parallel computing: parallel architecture, algorithms, software, and problem-solving techniques. Areas covered: Flynn’s taxonomy, processor-memory organizations, shared and nonshared memory models: message passing and multithreading, data parallelism; speedup, efficiency and Amdahl’s law, communication and synchronization, isoefficiency and scalability. Assignments given to provide practical experience.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 100 or CSE 100R; restricted to CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Computer Graphics
courses.description: Representation and manipulation of pictorial data. Two-dimensional and three-dimensional transformations, curves, surfaces. Projection, illumination, and shading models. Raster and vector graphic I/O devices; retained-mode and immediate-mode graphics software systems and applications. Students may not receive credit for CSE 167 and CSE 167R or MATH 155A.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 100 or CSE 100R; restricted to CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Computer Animation
courses.description: Advanced graphics focusing on the programming techniques involved in computer animation. Algorithms and approaches for both character animation and physically based animation. Particular subjects may include skeletons, skinning, key framing, facial animation, inverse kinematics, locomotion, motion capture, video game animation, particle systems, rigid bodies, clothing, and hair. Recommended preparation: an understanding of linear algebra.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 167 or CSE 167R; restricted to CS25, CS26, CS27, CS29, and EC26 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Molecular Sequence Analysis
courses.description: This course covers the analysis of nucleic acid and protein sequences, with an emphasis on the application of algorithms to biological problems. Topics include sequence alignments, database searching, comparative genomics, and phylogenetic and clustering analyses. Pairwise alignment, multiple alignment, DNS sequencing, scoring functions, fast database search, comparative genomics, clustering, phylogenetic trees, gene finding/DNA statistics.
courses.prerequisites_text: CSE 100 or CSE 100R and CSE 101 and BIMM 100 or CHEM 114C; restricted to BE28, BI34, CH37, and CS27 majors. Students may receive credit for one of the following: CSE 181, BIMM 181, BENG 181, or CSE 181R.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Topics in Computer Science and Engineering
courses.description: Topics of special interest in computer science and engineering. Topics may vary from quarter to quarter. May be repeated for credit with the consent of instructor. May be taken for credit up to three times. May be coscheduled with CSE 291.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor. Department stamp required.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Seminar in CSE
courses.description: A seminar course on topics of current interest. Students, as well as the instructor, will be actively involved in running the course/class. This course cannot be counted toward a technical elective.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor. Department stamp required.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Field Study in Computer Science and Engineering
courses.description: Directed study accompanying full-time on-site computer science internships. (P/NP grades only.)
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of the instructor and approval of the department required. Students may receive credit for one of the following: CSE 197 or CSE 197C. Restricted to CS25, CS26, CS27, and CS29 majors only.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Directed Group Study
courses.description: Computer science and engineering topics whose study involves reading and discussion by a small group of students under the supervision of a faculty member. (P/NP grades only.)
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of the instructor. Department stamp required.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Independent Study for Undergraduates
courses.description: Independent reading or research by special arrangement with a faculty member. (P/NP grades only.)
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of the instructor. Department stamp required.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: CSE Honors Thesis Research for Undergraduates
courses.description: Undergraduate research for completing an honors project under the supervision of a CSE faculty member. May be taken across multiple quarters. Students should enroll for a letter grade. May be taken for credit three times.
courses.prerequisites_text: Admission to the CSE department honors program. Consent of the instructor. Department stamp required.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Algorithm Design and Analysis
courses.description: The basic techniques for the design and analysis of algorithms. Divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, data structures, graph search, algebraic problems, randomized algorithms, lower bounds, probabilistic analysis, parallel algorithms. Recommended preparation: Understanding of design and analysis of efficient algorithms with emphasis of nonnumerical algorithms such as sorting, searching, pattern matching, and graph and network algorithms. Restricted to students within the CS75, CS78, CS89, CS88, CS77, CS80, CS81, CS83, and CS76 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Convex Optimization Formulations and Algorithms
courses.description: We study the formulations and algorithms solving convex optimization problems. The topics include convex sets, functions, optimality conditions, duality concepts, gradient descent, conjugate gradient, interior-point methods, and applications. The objective of the course is to provide students the background and techniques for scientific computing and system optimization. Students cannot receive credit for CSE 203B if they have taken either ECE 273 or MATH 245B. Recommended preparation: Linear algebra is recommended. Restricted to students within the CS75, CS78, CS89, CS88, CS77, CS80, CS81, CS83, and CS76 majors. All other students will be allowed as space permits.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Topics/Seminar in Algorithms, Complexity, and Logic
courses.description: Topics of special interest in algorithms, complexity, and logic to be presented by faculty and students under faculty direction. Topics vary from quarter to quarter. May be repeated for credit.
courses.prerequisites_text: consent of instructor.

courses.subject: CSE
courses.title: Principles of Software Engineering
courses.description: (Formerly CSE 264A.) General principles in modern software engineering. Both theoretical and practical topics are covered. Theoretical topics include proofs of correctness, programming language semantics, and theory of testing.
